title: All things have their season
paragraphs: Those who compare Cato the Censor with the younger Cato, who killed himself, are comparing two fine natures, much alike. The first earned his reputation in various ways, and stands out for his military exploits and the usefulness of his public service; but the virtue of the younger Cato, quite apart from the fact that it would be blasphemy to set anything beside it in strength, was much purer and unblemished. For who could acquit the Censor of envy and ambition, when he dared to attack the honour of Scipio, a man in goodness and every other excellent quality infinitely beyond him or anyone else of his time?

What they report of him, among other things — that in his extreme old age he took to learning Greek with so eager an appetite, as though to quench a long thirst — does not seem to me to be much in his favour; it is really what we would call lapsing into a second childhood. All things have their season, even good ones, and I may say my Paternoster at the wrong time; as they reproached T. Quintus Flaminius for having been seen praying off to one side while general of an army, during the battle he won.
["The wise man limits even honest things." — Juvenal, vi. 444]

Eudemonidas, seeing Xenocrates, very old, still busy with his lectures, said, "When will this man be wise, if he is still learning?" And Philopoemen, to those who praised King Ptolemy for putting his body through arms drill every day, said, "It is not commendable in a king of his age to be exercising in these things; he ought now actually to be using them." The young, say the sages, are to make their preparations, the old to enjoy them; and the greatest fault they see in us is that our desires keep renewing themselves and growing young again — we are always starting to live over.
Our studies and our desires should feel their age; yet here we are with one foot in the grave, and still our appetites and pursuits keep springing up fresh inside us:
"Tu secanda marmora Locas sub ipsum funus, et, sepulcri Immemor, struis domos."
["You against the time of death have marble cut for use, and, forgetful of the tomb, build houses." — Horace, Od., ii. 18, 17.]

The longest of my designs does not stretch beyond a year. My thoughts are now only of finishing; I am ridding myself of every new hope and project, taking my last leave of every place I leave, and every day dispossessing myself of what I have.
"Olim jam nec perit quicquam mihi, nec acquiritur.... plus superest viatici quam viae."

["Henceforward I will neither lose, nor expect to get: I have more wherewith to defray my journey, than I have way to go." (Or): "Hitherto nothing of me has been lost or gained; more remains to pay the way than there is way." — Seneca, Ep., 77. (The sense seems to be that so far he had met his expenses, but that for the future he was likely to have more than he required.)]
"Vixi, et, quem dederat cursum fortuna, peregi."
["I have lived and finished the career Fortune placed before me." — Aeneid, iv. 653.]

Indeed this is the one comfort I find in my old age, that it deadens in me several of the cares and desires that troubled my life: the care of how the world goes, the care of wealth, of grandeur, of knowledge, of health, of myself. There are men who are learning to speak when they should be learning to be silent for good. A man can always study, but he must not always be in school: what a pitiable thing is an old man at his ABCs.
"Diversos diversa juvant; non omnibus annis Omnia conveniunt."
["Various things delight various men; all things are not for all ages." — Gall., Eleg., i. 104.]

If we must study, let us study what fits our present condition, so that we can answer as that man did who, being asked to what end he was studying in his decrepit age, replied, "That I may go out the better, and the more at my ease." Such was the study of the younger Cato, when he felt his end approaching, and which he met with in Plato's discourse on the eternity of the soul — not, as we should think, that he was not long since equipped with every kind of provision for such a departure; for in steadiness, settled will, and instruction he had more than Plato has in all his writings; his knowledge and his courage were, on this point, above philosophy. He applied himself to this study, not for the sake of his death, but as a man whose sleep was never broken by the importance of such a decision, who without choice or change went on with his studies along with the other usual activities of his life. The night he was refused the praetorship he spent in play; the night he was to die he spent in reading. The loss of life or of office was all one to him.
